digest.intro: Dead networks, trapped antimatter, and 200,000 missing creative jobs.

sections.heading: The creative class and the labor question

items.title: AI and the Fall of the Creative Class
items.blurb: 200,000 creative jobs gone in four years, 50,000 in the last year alone — a pace of loss that historically only appeared during full recessions, except there's no recession. The sharpest signal that AI is the driver rather than consolidation alone: every subsector of digital creative work is contracting simultaneously, while in-person entertainment (concerts, live events) is still growing. Film and TV have shed roughly a third of their workforce; publishing 70,000 jobs. The piece is careful about what it can and can't prove, which makes the parts it does assert land harder.

items.title: MIT X-Hinges: Sensors Baked Into the Print, Not Bolted On
items.blurb: X-Hinges is design software that embeds contact sensors directly into 3D printed objects during fabrication — lamps, gloves, hinges — so the object itself perceives and responds to touch without any added electronics. The sensor geometry is generated as part of the print path, not as an afterthought. This is the physical/digital seam moving inward: the thing knows you're touching it because sensing is structural, not attached.

items.title: The Löffelholz Codex: A 1505 Maker's Manual Nobody Has Ever Fully Read
items.blurb: In 1505, a Nuremberg knight began sketching everything that occupied his mind: drills with interchangeable blades, a workbench vise, a swivel chair on casters, a crossbow disassembled into all its parts, a cradle whose rockers are filled with mercury. The book has 154 pages, is fully digitized, is in the public domain — and in 500 years no one has ever produced a complete transcription or translation. A team is going through it page by page now, with engineering annotations, and it's browsable as they work.

items.title: Why Gopher in 2026?
items.blurb: Someone is writing a phlog — a blog on Gopher, the pre-web protocol from 1991, still running, still attracting people who want a network with no tracking, no ads, no algorithmic surface, no corporate interest — and the opening question is genuinely worth sitting with: what does it mean that teenagers with ADHD are gravitating toward flip phones and dead protocols to escape the noise? The author notices that constraint is the point, not the limitation. The HN thread around it gets into the cultural logic more cleanly than most essays about digital minimalism ever do.

items.title: Physicists Trapped a Single Antimatter Particle for a Month
items.blurb: The team starts with sodium-22, a radioactive isotope that emits a positron when it decays, then slows that positron down by sending it through the crystal lattice of cold tungsten — essentially pinballing it until it loses enough energy to catch. Holding a single antihydrogen atom in a magnetic trap for 30 days is a precision measurement achievement that opens the question of whether antimatter and matter obey identical physical laws. If they don't, that asymmetry is likely why the universe is made of matter at all and not an equal mix of both that annihilated itself at the start.

facts.fact: The Löffelholz Codex — a 154-page illustrated tool book from 1505 featuring a mercury-filled rocking cradle and a swivel chair on casters — has never been fully transcribed or translated in over 500 years.

Samsung TVs are silently running AlexNet (a TensorFlow Lite model named 'alex.tflite') on 960×540 camera captures every few seconds to identify what game you're playing — before any consent screen appears.

Physicists slow antimatter positrons by sending them through the crystal lattice of cold tungsten, where they lose energy by colliding with atoms — a technique that made month-long magnetic trapping of a single antihydrogen atom possible.

art_picks.title: Daughters of the Dust
art_picks.creator: Julie Dash
art_picks.why: The first feature film by a Black woman theatrically distributed in the US — shot in Gullah communities of the Sea Islands in 1991, it's less a narrative than a system: a feedback loop of memory, myth, and matrilineal continuity told through image and rhythm rather than plot. The way Dash builds meaning from fabric, light, and gesture — pure visual semiotics — will make a maker want to go make something immediately.

art_picks.title: Krasner and Pollock: Past Continuous
art_picks.creator: Lee Krasner & Jackson Pollock
art_picks.why: The Met's current exhibition reframes the most mythologized relationship in American abstraction as a genuine dialogue rather than a footnote — surfacing the feedback loops between two practices that shaped each other in ways art history has systematically erased. Krasner's own work, seen in full, is a completely different and more interesting story than the one that got told.

art_picks.title: Quanta Qualia
art_picks.creator: Oren Ambarchi
art_picks.why: Ambarchi builds music the way a generative artist builds a system: one repeated guitar tone, layered with imperceptible precision until rhythm and texture become indistinguishable. It's obsessive, structural, and deeply physical — the kind of work that makes you rethink what a single instrument is even for. Especially relevant given his Blank Forms residency this week.

events.name: Arthur Jafa: I Am Tony
events.why: The largest survey of Jafa's work to date — four decades of film, video collage, sculpture, and photography assembled like a jazz drummer's edit: rhythm and juxtaposition as method, Black popular culture as structural framework, and the invisible systems of race and media as subject matter; exactly the kind of show that makes physical and digital, archive and gut-feeling, indistinguishable.

events.name: Tang Shuo: Borrowed History
events.why: A small-gallery solo at a sharp LES space — the title alone signals the kind of work Willem would want to see: art that treats history as raw material to be sampled and recontextualized, not preserved.

events.name: Cici Wu: Auld Lang Syne (Prelude)
events.why: 47 Canal consistently programs work at the intersection of language, systems, and material — Wu's practice deals in displacement, memory, and infrastructure as form, the kind of conceptually dense but sensory work that rewards a slow look.

events.name: Oren Ambarchi / Andrew Cyrille / Cyro Baptista — Night Two
events.venue: Blank Forms, 151 Lafayette St, 6th Floor, Manhattan
events.why: A first-ever trio encounter between Ambarchi's deep-drone guitar minimalism, Andrew Cyrille's free-jazz percussion mastery, and Cyro Baptista's Brazilian rhythmic invention — three distinct sound-worlds in one room, at one of NYC's most curatorially serious small venues; the kind of unrepeatable collision that only happens when someone books with real taste.

events.name: Ólafur Arnalds
events.venue: Town Hall Theater, 123 W 43rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Arnalds builds neo-classical systems from generative software and acoustic instruments simultaneously — live, his shows are less concerts than demonstrations of a feedback loop between composed and emergent, which lands differently when you're a builder who works at that same edge.

trial_sources.name: Global Inequality and More 3.0 — Branko Milanovic
trial_sources.why: A world-class economist writing sharp, short-form posts that cut across geopolitics, economic history, cultural capital, and global status hierarchies — exactly the kind of individual human with taste who sees the world's fault lines before institutions do.

trial_sources.name: The Niche — Paul Knoepfler
trial_sources.why: A UC Davis stem cell biologist who writes credible, independent expert commentary on regenerative medicine, iPSCs, peptides, and longevity research — the rare scientist-blogger who translates frontier research without hype.

trial_sources.name: Make Anything — Devin Montes
trial_sources.why: A designer-maker channel focused on the intersection of high-level 3D modeling, artistic fabrication, and the aesthetics of what additive manufacturing can produce — craft-minded and visually sophisticated, not just a gear-review channel.
